one_liner: Hands-on cyber incident responder in DHS's Cybersecurity Service: monitor networks, analyze logs and SIEM alerts, contain intrusions, and brief leaders. It fills a one-year talent pool.
fit_summary: This is a deeply technical cybersecurity role, and the posting says the track generally expects 5-15 years of cybersecurity work experience, including a proctored technical exam and a resume review requiring explicit cyber experience. Nothing on file shows Daniel has cybersecurity experience. Daniel's emergency-management consulting and communication strengths fit the incident-coordination and after-action reporting pieces, but those alone won't pass Phase II.
eligibility: Open to the public (hiring path: public), so U.S. citizens without federal status may apply.
Technical Track generally expects 5-15 years of cybersecurity work experience, and the resume must explicitly outline cybersecurity experience after Phase II.
Requires eligibility for a Top Secret/SCI (Sensitive Compartmented Information) clearance.
No degree is required, but you must pass both Phase I online assessments and the proctored Phase II Mitigation and Response technical assessment at a designated center.
Duty location is listed as Multiple Locations and the job is not telework-eligible or remote, so confirm DC-area slots exist.
strategy: Be honest with yourself first: apply only if you have real, explainable hands-on cyber work (SOC, IT security, log analysis), because Phase II tests technical skill and the resume review checks explicit cybersecurity experience.

If you have no cyber background, treat this as a target for later. Instead, look at FEMA, CISA, or DHS emergency-management, preparedness, policy, or stakeholder-engagement roles that fit your IEM experience now.

If you do apply, frame your IEM work around incident coordination, continuity/recovery planning, after-action reports, and briefing government leaders. Use the posting's exact language, but only where it is accurate.
Phase I measures communication, analysis, and collaboration, not cyber knowledge, so take it in a quiet setting with audio and reserve the full 2 hours for the work simulation.
The window runs October 29 to November 13, 2026. Watch your email closely after applying, because the assessment deadlines are time-sensitive and Phase II must be scheduled at a proctored center.
Keep the resume to the two-page USAJOBS limit. List the dates and hours per week for each job, and put any cybersecurity duties first under each role.
resume_bullets: Supported [government client] [incident/disaster response] operations at IEM by coordinating [number] stakeholders and producing situational updates and after-action reports for [leadership level].
Developed [recovery action plans / continuity plans] for [client], integrating stakeholder feedback to identify vulnerabilities and recommend mitigation strategies.
[If applicable] Monitored and analyzed [log sources/SIEM tool] to identify indicators of compromise and escalated [number] incidents per NIST incident handling guidelines, [hours/week].
interview_questions: Walk us through how you would handle a suspected intrusion from detection to recovery using NIST incident handling stages.
How would you brief a senior executive versus a SOC team on the same incident?
Describe a time you coordinated with multiple stakeholders under pressure during an incident or emergency.
Which SIEM or endpoint security tools have you used, and how?
watch_outs: The role requires substantial cybersecurity experience and a proctored technical exam, which is a major gap unless Daniel has unlisted cyber work.
The position requires a TS/SCI clearance, which means a lengthy background investigation.
There is no telework, and the location is Multiple Locations, so placement could be outside Northern Virginia.
Applying places you in a talent pool rather than guaranteeing a job, and the pay level is set by assessed experience.
